title: The Tree of Hope and a Brooklyn gangster nightclub with Hilton Jefferson
summary: Benny James introduced him under the Tree of Hope to Hilton Jefferson, who offered a Brooklyn job in a lazy six-piece band under a Cuban or Puerto Rican trumpeter.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I know exactly what it was, too. I was standing around at 131st Street where the Tree of Hope used to be. That's what it was, a tree there. They called it the Tree of Hope. Broken-down axes and things. You know, it means superstitious. They're going to stand under that tree and rub that tree. They'd rub that tree, you know.
Yeah.
Well, that's why they called it the Tree of Hope. Well, I was standing under that tree, leaning on it.
Holmes (10/9) - 68
The job had just closed, Chez Paree or Chez Florence just closed, and I'm standing under there.

And a fellow, Benny James, a guitar player, he walks up to me, and he's pulling Hilton Jefferson with him, he's got him by the hand. He said, "Here's the man. This is the man you want. This man." He's pointing at me, you know. So he introduced Hilton Jefferson to me, which I knew Hilton but I didn't know him to speak to. He introduced me, and Hilton Jefferson asked me did I want a job. I says, "Yeah, I ain't doin' nothing." He said, "Well, I have a job in Brooklyn, at a nightclub in Brooklyn. If you want it, you can start tonight." "Well, that's beautiful" -- because I wasn't doin' nothin'. So he told me what time to be there, this, that and the other.

And this other fellow, Benny James, was on the job, and ...(?)... So we go over there together, to the job. Well, this place was run by gangsters, naturally. It was all right with me. I liked to work with gangsters.

Anyway, it wasn't a hard job. We just went in and played whatever they wanted to hear. And we'd play about a half-hour, get up and go into the back of the club, and you know, do anything we wanted to do. Then come back and play some more. Nobody bothered you. And it got sort of routine, you know. So...
Holmes (10/9) - 69
This was what? A nightclub, dancing...
This was a nightclub, yeah.
The patrons were dancing?
Yeah. Dancing and drinking whiskey.
So it was basically a dance band that you were...

No. The band was just about six musicians, that's all, sitting up there. And they were so lazy... The trumpet player was the leader. His name Cohen(?), and he was Puerto Rican or Cuban... I don't know whether he was Cuban or Puerto Rican. But usually they're pretty ambitious people, but he was a lazy one. He could play, but he didn't want to play. He wasn't interested in nothin'. Just "Let's get the night over with." That's all he wanted. And get away from there.

There were a couple of others in the band... They didn't care nothin' about music. It was just a job, that's all. The piano player, he was a good piano player, but stayed drunk all the time. He drank all the time. But he was a good piano player. And he wanted to always talk, and he'd be slobberin' and carryin' on, and couldn't nobody understand what he was saying. "Yah, bah-bah," he was talkin' all over the place.
I mean, musically speaking, it didn't mean nothin'. Because I stayed there the whole summer... Not the whole
Holmes (10/9) - 70
summer there, because in the summer-time, in July, they moved to Rockaway Beach -- they had a place down there. We stayed down there. Then in the Fall, they come back to this place in Brooklyn.

But the band was nothing to improve or anything. We played the same numbers every night, and... The leader didn't want to play nothin'. Nobody else wanted to play nothin'. The guitar player, he couldn't play nothin'. I mean, it was just... You know what I mean? And sometimes I'd get a new riff, I'd play a new riff (?), and everybody would wake up. They didn't care one way or the other, you know. I mean, you lose ambition. And at that time, I was very ambitious. I wanted to be good.
